tasks_in_class.description: Write the number for each donation quantity shown as Dienes blocks, '4 Ones + 7 Tens', bundles, '100–7', and grids.
Write the time and draw HTO blocks for 52, 145, 325, and 508 people at different time slots; identify the time slot with most and least people.
Make 3-digit numbers using digits 3 and 7; write them in boxes, circle the smallest, and cross out the largest.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the langar donation context. Children read Let Us Do, p.39–40 ("Write the number for each donation quantity shown as Dienes blocks….") — working through block pictures, bundle diagrams, the expression '4 Ones + 7 Tens', and the grid form, writing the matching number for each.

Children move to Let Us Do, p.40–41 ("Write the time and draw HTO blocks for 52, 145, 325….") — sketching Dienes blocks for each crowd count and circling the busiest and quietest time slot. Pairs compare drawings and discuss how the hundred-flat, ten-rod, and unit-square map onto the digits.

Children tackle Let Us Do Q1(a), p.41 ("Make 3-digit numbers using digits 3 and 7….") — listing all arrangements, writing them in the boxes, then circling the smallest and crossing out the largest. Bring the class together to share answers and reason about why position of digits changes value.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse the value of a digit with its face value — watch for a child who writes '4 Ones + 7 Tens' as 47 rather than 74. Connecting the Dienes rod (ten-stick) and flat (hundred-square) to their column in the HTO table helps ground this. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q1(b)–Q1(c) and Q2, p.41–42, can be assigned for reinforcement.
materials: Dienes block sets (or printed block cut-outs)

tasks_in_class.description: Count the full number chart up to 1100 to find how many people came for the community lunch; fill in blanks continuing the sequence beyond 1000.
Identify the number range (Only 1 to More than 1000) most suitable for each situation (leaves in a tree, books in classroom, ants in anthill, etc.) and name things around you that exceed 1000.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the langar number chart. Ask children how many squares are on the chart and let them make quick estimates before counting. Briefly share real-world contexts (Thousand Pillars Temple, rhinoceros population) to anchor the size of one thousand in familiar images.

Children work on p.43 ("Count the full number chart up to 1100 to find how many people came….") — counting the chart in sections with a partner, then filling the blanks to continue the sequence past 1000. Circulate and prompt: 'What comes after 999? After 1009?'

Children attempt Q3, p.44 ("Identify the number range most suitable for each situation….") — matching each real-life quantity to its range band and then naming objects around them that exceed 1000. Share examples as a class, building a collective list on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is writing 'one thousand' as '10000' (adding an extra zero) because children hear 'ten hundred'. Explicitly linking the completed chart — 100 squares filled ten times — to the single symbol 1000 counteracts this. Encourage children to use the Indian number system's history (introduced in the chapter) to discuss why ten symbols are enough to write every number.
materials: board or large chart paper for class list

section_titles: Breaking up One Thousand — complements and addition facts
periods.activity_title: Building the Thousand Cube and Breaking It Apart

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Break Up One-Thousand (a)–(f), p.47
tasks_in_class.description: Mark 900, 800, 850, 760, 400 on the Dienes-hundreds number line and find how much more/less each is from 1000; complete eight addition facts of the form ___ + ___ = 1000.

time_bands.activity: Use Dienes blocks (or drawn pictures) to show the times-10 chain: 10 unit-squares make a rod, 10 rods make a flat, 10 flats make the thousand-cube. Children group and regroup physical or drawn blocks at their desks, confirming each step before moving to the next. Draw the four pieces on the board labelled 1, 10, 100, 1000.

Children open to p.47 and work through Let Us Break Up One-Thousand (a)–(f) ("Mark 900, 800, 850, 760, 400 on the Dienes-hundreds number line….") — placing each number on the vertical hundreds line, writing how far it is from 1000, and completing the eight orange-segment addition facts. Pairs check each other's complement calculations.

periods.teacher_notes: The grouping chain — 10 ones = 1 ten, 10 tens = 1 hundred, 10 hundreds = 1 thousand — is the structural spine the rest of the chapter rests on; unhurried hands-on grouping here prevents procedural errors later. Watch for children who find the complement by subtraction (1000 − 760 = 240) rather than counting up — both are valid and worth discussing. S3 has no listed tasks; the Dienes block visualisation is delivered through the hands-on opening band before moving to the complement task in S4.
materials: Dienes block sets or printed cut-outs

section_titles: Grouping and Regrouping with Dienes pictures
periods.activity_title: Circling Tens and Hundreds: Regrouping in Pictures

tasks_in_class.description: Look at Dienes pictures; circle groups of 10 Ones or 10 Tens as many times as possible; write expanded form (Tens + Ones or Hundreds + Tens + Ones) and the final number for two pictures.
Identify and write the standard numbers for: 45 Ones, 39 Ones, 35 Tens, 86 Tens, 10T+1O, 15T+23O, 34T+12O, 19T+10O, 2H+13T+7O.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.48 ("Look at Dienes pictures; circle groups of 10 Ones or 10 Tens….") — working on the two pictures, drawing circles around groups of ten units or ten rods, then writing the expanded form and the final number. Pairs share their circling strategies; discuss why 'leftover' pieces after grouping become the Ones or Tens digit.

Children move to Let Us Solve (a)–(i), p.50 ("Identify and write the standard numbers for: 45 Ones, 39 Ones….") — working independently to regroup each non-canonical expression into standard form, using mental grouping since no pictures are provided. Circulate; spotlight two contrasting examples (e.g. '35 Tens = 350' and '2H+13T+7O = 337') to consolidate the rule.

periods.teacher_notes: The p.49 tasks (T-11) give a pictorial bridge between p.48 and p.50; if time allows at the close of the symbolic work, direct children to p.49 as an intermediate check. The most common error is treating '15 Tens' as 15 rather than regrouping to 150 — ask 'How many ones is one ten worth?' to redirect. Additional practice: p.49 tasks can be completed as reinforcement.

section_titles: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
periods.activity_title: The Thousands Column: Tokens, Tables, and Sequences

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the Tokens–Expanded Form–Th–H–T–O–Number–Number Name table for multiple rows including numbers from 1001 to 3019.
Write numbers in sequence forward and backward: (a) starting at 1027, 1028…; (b) starting at …2008, 2009…

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Thousands column using a Dienes thousand-cube picture or drawn on the board. Show the token shorthand — a coloured chip for 1000 — and relate it to the 100-chip, 10-chip, and 1-chip already familiar from HTO work. Write one 4-digit number (e.g. 2345) in the THTO table together as a class.

Children fill the Tokens–Expanded Form–Th–H–T–O–Number–Number Name table on p.52–53 ("Fill in the table for multiple rows including numbers from 1001 to 3019") — working row by row, reading token pictures, writing expanded form, and writing the number name. Partners compare number names, discussing how 'one thousand three hundred and seven' maps to 1307.

Children complete Q1(a)–(b), p.53 ("Write numbers in sequence forward and backward: starting at 1027….") — continuing and reversing each sequence, then reading their sequences aloud to a partner to check. Discuss: 'What happens to the tens digit as we count from 1029 to 1030?'

periods.teacher_notes: The Thousands column is new; children need to hear and say the number names aloud (not just write them) to solidify the spoken form. A frequent slip is omitting the zero placeholder — 1030 written as 130 — which the Let Us Think task addresses directly; note examples that arise here for that discussion. Encourage children to check their number names by pointing to each digit in the THTO table.
materials: coloured token chips or cut-out tokens

section_titles: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
periods.activity_title: Slider Game, Zero Placeholder, and Token Regrouping

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Play (place value slider) (a)–(e), p.54
tasks_in_class.description: Make the place value slider and take turns to increase or decrease: 1895 by 1, 2785 by 10, 3369 by 2, 5648 by 10, 6487 by 20.
Decide whether Ram's writing of 7Th 0H 2T 4O as 724 is correct; write the correct number. Do the same for Richa's 5Th 6H 0T 3O written as 563.
Use tokens to identify and write in the Th-H-T-O table: 6T+22O, 4T+12O, 3H+14T+8O, 12H+18T+2O, 1Th+5H+10T+17O.

time_bands.activity: Children make the place value slider (cut and assemble per p.54 instructions) and work through Let Us Play (a)–(e) ("Make the place value slider and take turns to increase or decrease: 1895 by 1….") — partners take turns sliding and reading aloud the result. Focus attention on cases where increasing by 10 changes the tens AND hundreds digit.

Children read Let Us Think Q1–2, p.54 ("Decide whether Ram's writing of 7Th 0H 2T 4O as 724 is correct….") — writing their verdict and the correct number for both Ram and Richa. Discuss as a class: 'What does the zero in the hundreds place actually do? What would happen if we left it out?'

Children complete Let Us Solve Q1(a)–(e), p.57 ("Use tokens to identify and write in the Th-H-T-O table: 6T+22O….") — regrouping each non-canonical token expression into the standard four-column form. Spotlight 12H+18T+2O to show multi-level regrouping.

periods.teacher_notes: The zero-as-placeholder error — dropping zeros from middle columns — is the chapter's most significant misconception; Let Us Think isolates it explicitly and the class discussion is the teaching moment. The slider makes the positional nature of digits felt rather than just seen. Additional practice: Let Us Solve 2A and 2B, p.57 (T-18, T-19), can be used for quick oral comparison work if time permits.
materials: Place value slider materials (card strips, p.54)

section_titles: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
periods.activity_title: Arrow Cards, Find Me Grid, and Comparison Pairs

tasks_in_class.description: Use arrow cards to make numbers like 3452 and 4085; read aloud each number and express it in expanded form and in words.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Play (Find Me! grid), p.56
tasks_in_class.description: Read aloud eight clues (e.g. 'the number 3782', 'a 4-digit number with all digits the same') and locate the matching numbers in the digit grid.
Circle the bigger number in each pair: 30 or 300; 6000 or 600; 6000 or 3000.

time_bands.activity: Distribute arrow card sets. Children work through Let Us Play (arrow cards), p.56 ("Use arrow cards to make numbers like 3452 and 4085….") — assembling each number, reading it aloud, then writing the expanded form and the number name. Emphasise that the zero card for '0 hundreds' must be placed and then slid under the thousands card.

Children open to the Find Me! grid on p.56 ("Read aloud eight clues… and locate the matching numbers in the digit grid") — working in pairs, one reading the clue and the other scanning the grid. Encourage children to articulate why a given number matches a clue like 'all digits the same'.

Children complete Let Us Solve 2A, p.57 ("Circle the bigger number in each pair: 30 or 300….") — working quickly and orally justifying each choice using the number of digits or the leading digit. Use Let Us Solve 2B (T-19) as an oral stretch for children who finish rapidly.

periods.teacher_notes: Arrow cards physically separate place-value components and reassemble them, making expanded form tactile rather than purely symbolic — this is especially valuable for children who rush number writing without attending to position. A common error in the Find Me grid is confusing 'all digits the same' with 'all digits are zero'; ask children to name a concrete example first. Additional practice: Let Us Solve 2B, p.57, can be completed as quiet follow-up.
materials: Arrow card sets (cut-out, p.56 or prepared)

periods.activity_title: Placing Thousands on the Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Mark given 4-digit numbers on number lines: 1043/1069/1084 on a 1000–1100 line; 2025–2460 on a 2000–2500 line; 5512–5695 on a 5500–5725 line; 8679/8990/8923/8763 on an 8500–9000 line.

time_bands.activity: Open with a class discussion: 'Without a line, how do you know whether 3236 is between 2226 and 3226?' Then children work through Number Line Q1, p.55 ("Circle which of {3316, 3236, 2236, 2216, 3126, 3216} lie between 2226 and 3226") — writing a brief reason beside each circled number using the THTO comparison method.

Children work through Number Line Q2(a)–(d), p.55 ("Mark given 4-digit numbers on number lines: 1043/1069/1084 on a 1000–1100 line….") — tackling all four lines, first counting the interval size, then estimating the position before marking. Pairs compare placements on the 5500–5725 line (interval 25) and discuss any differences.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often place numbers by digit count alone rather than by magnitude, leading to errors on lines with unequal intervals. Asking 'How many equal jumps fit between the two ends?' before marking helps calibrate estimation. The progression from intervals of 10 to intervals of 125 in Q2 is deliberate — resist the urge to skip to the harder lines.

periods.activity_title: Comparing with Tokens and the THTO Table

tasks_in_class.description: Compare 3012 and 3102 using the THTO table; describe which position (Th, H, T, O) helped decide which is bigger.
Compare pairs using < or >: 2190/2910, 7087/7088, 1009/9001, 982/1024. Make a THTO table if needed.
Order the prices ₹1986, ₹1099, ₹1899 from smallest to biggest and fill in the < signs.

time_bands.activity: Read the Gurudwara plate-count context (p.58) together. Children work through the comparison of 3012 and 3102 on p.58 ("Compare 3012 and 3102 using the THTO table….") — filling the table and identifying aloud which column resolved the comparison. Draw out the rule: 'Start from the left; stop at the first column that differs.'

Children complete Let Us Do Q1(a)–(d), p.59 ("Compare pairs using < or >: 2190/2910….") — using the THTO table for any pair where they are uncertain, and writing the < or > symbol. Discuss Q1(d) (982 vs 1024) as a class: a 3-digit number is always smaller than a 4-digit number.

Children work through Let Us Do Q2, p.59 ("Order the prices ₹1986, ₹1099, ₹1899 from smallest to biggest….") — arranging the three prices in ascending order and filling in the < signs. Invite a child to explain the step-by-step comparison aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The comparison of 3012 and 3102 is the chapter's worked example for the column-by-column rule; it is worth slowing down on it. A common error is comparing numbers digit by digit from right to left rather than left to right — the THTO table layout, with Thousands on the left, helps redirect this. Additional practice: p.58 token comparison (T-24) can be done as a quick warm-up by reading the token pictures aloud.

periods.activity_title: Ordering Scores, Heights, and Open-Ended Comparisons

tasks_in_class.description: Arrange five women cricketers' ODI run totals (Debbie Hockley 4064, Suzie Bates 5114, Karen Rolton 4814, Mithali Raj 7805, Charlotte 6002) in increasing order.
Arrange seven mountain ranges (including K2 8611 m, Kangchenjunga 8586 m, Nanda Devi 7816 m, and others) in decreasing order of height.
Fill the blanks with digits 0–9 so the inequalities hold: 7_ _3 < 768_; 853_ < 8_3_; _2_1 < 5_2_.

time_bands.activity: Children work through Let Us Do Q3, p.59 ("Arrange five women cricketers' ODI run totals… in increasing order") — writing the five scores in a THTO table, then ordering them. Discuss: 'Did any two scores have the same thousands digit? How did you break the tie?'

Children complete Let Us Do Q4, p.60 ("Arrange seven mountain ranges… in decreasing order of height") — listing heights in the THTO table and ordering from tallest to shortest. Draw attention to closely ranked pairs like K2 (8611) and Kangchenjunga (8586) to reinforce hundreds-column comparison.

Children attempt Let Us Do Q6(a)–(c), p.60 ("Fill the blanks with digits 0–9 so the inequalities hold: 7_ _3 < 768_….") — working in pairs to find valid digits, checking each choice by comparing the resulting numbers. Invite pairs to share different valid answers for Q6(b) and Q6(c).

periods.teacher_notes: Ordering more than two numbers benefits from writing them column-by-column in a shared table; children who try to compare in their heads often lose track of partial results. For Q6, the open nature of the digit-fill invites trial-and-improvement thinking — let children articulate 'if I put 9 here, the left side is 7993 and the right is 7689, so that fails' before they find the correct digit. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q5(a)–(f), p.60 (T-30), can be assigned as reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Challenge, Explore, and the Full Set of Permutations

tasks_in_class.description: How many whole numbers are strictly between 7000 and 8000? Circle from 900, 999, or 1000.
Make as many four-digit numbers as possible using digits 2, 3, 4, 7 without repetition (24 possible); arrange in decreasing order; compare with classmates to find all 24.

time_bands.activity: Children read CHALLENGE!, p.61 ("How many whole numbers are strictly between 7000 and 8000? Circle from 900, 999, or 1000") — jotting their reasoning before circling. Discuss as a class: list 7001, 7002, …, 7999 and count the range; connect to the number-line picture of a thousand-unit span.

Children work through Let Us Explore Q1–2, p.61 ("Make as many four-digit numbers as possible using digits 2, 3, 4, 7 without repetition….") — first listing numbers independently, then arranging them in decreasing order, and finally pooling lists with a neighbouring pair to check that all 24 are found. Each group reads their ordered list aloud to confirm.

periods.teacher_notes: For the CHALLENGE, children who answer 999 typically confuse 'strictly between' with 'from 7000 to 8000 inclusive' — ask them to count from 7001 to check. In the exploration task, a systematic approach (fix the thousands digit, list all arrangements of the remaining three) reliably produces all 24 numbers; model this only if a group is stuck after a genuine attempt. This unit completes all sections of the chapter; the synthesis unit draws on all the content taught here.

section_titles: Breaking up One Thousand — complements and addition facts
Grouping and Regrouping with Dienes pictures
Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
periods.activity_title: Thousands Around Us: Putting the Whole Chapter Together

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Break Up One-Thousand (a)–(f), p.47
tasks_in_class.description: Mark 900, 800, 850, 760, 400 on the Dienes-hundreds number line and find how much more/less each is from 1000; complete eight addition facts of the form ___ + ___ = 1000.
Decide whether Ram's writing of 7Th 0H 2T 4O as 724 is correct; write the correct number. Do the same for Richa's 5Th 6H 0T 3O written as 563.
Make as many four-digit numbers as possible using digits 2, 3, 4, 7 without repetition (24 possible); arrange in decreasing order; compare with classmates to find all 24.

time_bands.activity: Open with a rapid oral sweep across the chapter: ask children to tell you what '1000' looks like in Dienes blocks, how to write 'seven thousand, zero hundreds, two tens, four ones', and what the THTO table is for. Accept answers and connect them into the grouping chain — 10 ones → 1 ten → 1 hundred → 1 thousand — that underpins every section.

Revisit Let Us Think Q1–2, p.54 ("Decide whether Ram's writing of 7Th 0H 2T 4O as 724 is correct….") — this time as a whole-class demonstration. Write a new erroneous number on the board (e.g. 5 Th 0 H 0 T 9 O written as 59) and ask children to correct it and explain why the zeros must be written. Connect this to regrouping: '15 Tens and 23 Ones' regroups to 1 Hundred 7 Tens 3 Ones, not 1573.

Children work through Let Us Break Up One-Thousand (a)–(f), p.47 ("Mark 900, 800, 850, 760, 400 on the Dienes-hundreds number line….") as a timed review — filling in complement facts and confirming each with a neighbour. Draw the connection to the number-line work: a hundreds-line is a special case of the 4-digit number lines used in the number-line section.

Return to Let Us Explore Q1–2, p.61 ("Make as many four-digit numbers as possible using digits 2, 3, 4, 7 without repetition….") — small groups each take one thousands-digit (2, 3, 4, or 7) and list the six numbers that begin with it, arrange that group in decreasing order, and share with the class to build the full set of 24. Close by asking: 'Which section of this chapter helped you know how to order these?'

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws the full chapter together using the three threads that run through it: the grouping chain (ones→tens→hundreds→thousands), the zero-as-placeholder principle, and comparison by leftmost differing column. Choose the opening oral sweep questions based on which ideas seemed shakiest across earlier units. The systematic listing in the exploration task is itself a summary of place-value understanding — a child who can fix the thousands digit and enumerate the rest has genuinely grasped positional notation.
materials: p.47 and p.54 and p.61 in textbook

items.prompt: A number chart goes from 1 to 1000. Farida has filled rows 1 to 900. How many more numbers does she need to write to finish the chart? Show your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She needs to write 100 more numbers (from 901 to 1000).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count how many numbers are left: 1000 minus 900 equals 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child count on by tens from 900 to 1000 using fingers; stretch: ask how many rows of ten that makes.

exercise.description: Count the full number chart up to 1100 to find how many people came for the community lunch; fill in blanks continuing the sequence beyond 1000.

items.section_title: Grouping and Regrouping with Dienes pictures
items.prompt: A bag has 23 unit cubes. Circle groups of 10 in the picture below and write: ___ Tens and ___ Ones. Then write the number.
items.visual_stimulus:
| 10 cubes circled | 10 cubes circled | 3 loose cubes |
(Draw or imagine 23 unit squares arranged in a row.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 Tens and 3 Ones; the number is 23.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group 10 units into one ten twice; count the leftover units as ones.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw 23 squares and physically circle groups of 10; stretch: ask what happens if there are 32 unit cubes instead.

exercise.description: Look at Dienes pictures; circle groups of 10 Ones or 10 Tens as many times as possible; write expanded form (Tens + Ones or Hundreds + Tens + Ones) and the final number for two pictures.

items.section_title: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
items.prompt: Priya uses a place value slider. She starts at 3250 and increases the number by 10. What number does she get?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Adding 10 increases only the tens digit: 5 tens becomes 6 tens, giving 3260.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child increased the hundreds digit instead of the tens digit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child increased the thousands digit instead of the tens digit.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child increased the ones digit instead of the tens digit.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child write 3250 in the THTO table and change only the T column; stretch: ask what happens if they decrease 3260 by 10 three times.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Play (place value slider) (a)–(e), p.54
exercise.description: Make the place value slider and take turns to increase or decrease: 1895 by 1, 2785 by 10, 3369 by 2, 5648 by 10, 6487 by 20.

items.prompt: Using the digits 1, 5, 6, 9 (each used exactly once), write two different 4-digit numbers. Write them in decreasing order.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any valid decreasing pair, for example 9651 > 9615, or 9651 > 6951, etc. The larger number must appear first.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the thousands digit first; if equal, compare hundreds, then tens, then ones.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write both numbers in a THTO table and compare column by column; stretch: ask them to find the largest possible number they can make with those four digits.

exercise.description: Make as many four-digit numbers as possible using digits 2, 3, 4, 7 without repetition (24 possible); arrange in decreasing order; compare with classmates to find all 24.

items.prompt: A school hall has 325 chairs arranged in rows and columns shown as HTO blocks. The next day, 17 more chairs are added. Draw new HTO blocks to show the total and write the number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 342; the drawing should show 3 hundred-flats, 4 ten-rods, and 2 unit-squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add ones first (5 + 7 = 12, regroup to 1 ten and 2 ones), then add tens (2 + 1 + 1 = 4 tens).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw 325 blocks first, then add 17 loose units and regroup; stretch: ask what happens if 18 more chairs are added to 342.

exercise.description: Write the time and draw HTO blocks for 52, 145, 325, and 508 people at different time slots; identify the time slot with most and least people.

items.prompt: Using only the digits 3 and 7 (digits may repeat), which of the following is the smallest 3-digit number you can make?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the smallest digit in the hundreds position and in the tens position to get the smallest number.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child placed the smaller digit only in hundreds, not in tens.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child placed the larger digit in the hundreds position, giving the largest rather than smallest number.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child alternated digits without reasoning about which position most reduces the number's value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write each option in an HTO table and compare from the left; stretch: ask them to find the largest 3-digit number from the same two digits.

exercise.description: Make 3-digit numbers using digits 3 and 7; write them in boxes, circle the smallest, and cross out the largest.

items.prompt: Which number range best describes the number of pages in a thick storybook?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate the typical size of a thick storybook and match it to the range that contains reasonable page counts.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has not thought about realistic book sizes and chosen the smallest option.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child underestimates; 10–50 pages is closer to a thin picture book.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child overestimates; a thick storybook does not typically exceed 1000 pages.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to hold up a familiar book and count or estimate its pages in tens; stretch: ask them to name something that genuinely has more than 1000 of a kind.

exercise.description: Identify the number range (Only 1 to More than 1000) most suitable for each situation (leaves in a tree, books in classroom, ants in anthill, etc.) and name things around you that exceed 1000.

items.section_title: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
items.prompt: Sita writes 4 Thousands, 0 Hundreds, 3 Tens, and 6 Ones as 436. Is she correct? Write the correct number and explain the mistake.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sita is wrong. The correct number is 4036. She dropped the zero in the hundreds place, so her number only has three digits instead of four.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write each column value in the THTO table: Th=4, H=0, T=3, O=6, giving 4036.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to fill a THTO table with the given values and read across; stretch: ask them to write another 4-digit number with a zero in the tens place and check a neighbour's reading.

exercise.description: Decide whether Ram's writing of 7Th 0H 2T 4O as 724 is correct; write the correct number. Do the same for Richa's 5Th 6H 0T 3O written as 563.

items.prompt: Two numbers are 4028 and 4082. Write them in a THTO table and circle the bigger number. Which column helped you decide?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4082 is bigger. The thousands and hundreds columns are the same (4 and 0), so the tens column decides: 8 tens is greater than 2 tens.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare from the leftmost column; stop at the first column where the digits differ.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to cover thousands and hundreds and compare only tens; stretch: ask them to write a number between 4028 and 4082.

exercise.description: Compare 3012 and 3102 using the THTO table; describe which position (Th, H, T, O) helped decide which is bigger.

items.prompt: Four athletes' jump distances in centimetres are: 3812, 4210, 3921, 4021. Arrange them from smallest to biggest.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare thousands digits first; 3-thousand numbers come before 4-thousand numbers, then compare hundreds within each group.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write all four in a THTO table and sort by the Th column first; stretch: ask them to find the difference between the smallest and largest distance.

exercise.description: Arrange five women cricketers' ODI run totals (Debbie Hockley 4064, Suzie Bates 5114, Karen Rolton 4814, Mithali Raj 7805, Charlotte 6002) in increasing order.

items.prompt: How many whole numbers are strictly between 3000 and 4000?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Strictly between means 3000 and 4000 are excluded; count from 3001 to 3999, which is 3999 − 3001 + 1 = 999.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child counted only 900 numbers, perhaps stopping at 3900.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may have subtracted 2 from 1000, overcounting the exclusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child included one endpoint (3000 or 4000) in the count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to list 3001, 3002, … up to 3010 and count; stretch: ask how many whole numbers lie strictly between 5000 and 5010.

exercise.description: How many whole numbers are strictly between 7000 and 8000? Circle from 900, 999, or 1000.

items.prompt: Which number does '3 Hundreds + 0 Tens + 9 Ones' represent?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place each part in its column: H=3, T=0, O=9, reading across gives 309.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child swapped tens and ones, writing 90 where 09 belongs.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child ignored the hundreds value and wrote only the tens and ones.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child reversed the hundreds and ones digits.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write H, T, O on paper and fill each column; stretch: ask them to write 5 Hundreds + 0 Tens + 0 Ones and explain what the zeros mean.

exercise.description: Write the number for each donation quantity shown as Dienes blocks, '4 Ones + 7 Tens', bundles, '100–7', and grids.

items.section_title: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
items.prompt: A number has 2 Thousands, 4 Hundreds, 0 Tens, and 7 Ones. What is its number name?

options.label: C
options.text: Two thousand four hundred and seven

options.label: D
options.text: Two thousand four hundred and seventy

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two thousand four hundred and seven
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the THTO table left to right: 2 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones = two thousand four hundred and seven.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child read the zero tens as a ten, saying seventy instead of seven.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child ignored the hundreds digit and read only thousands, tens, and ones.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child used a non-standard name ('twenty-four hundred') not part of the Indian system taught in this chapter.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to fill in the THTO table and read each column aloud; stretch: ask them to write 2407 in expanded form.

exercise.description: Fill in the Tokens–Expanded Form–Th–H–T–O–Number–Number Name table for multiple rows including numbers from 1001 to 3019.

items.prompt: The number line below goes from 2000 to 2500 in steps of 100. Mark and label where 2300 and 2450 would go.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2300 is at the third tick (three steps of 100 from 2000); 2450 is halfway between the fourth tick (2400) and the fifth tick (2500).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each interval is 100; count the intervals from 2000 to locate each number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to label all the tick marks (2000, 2100, 2200, 2300, 2400, 2500) first; stretch: ask where 2375 would go and how they know.

exercise.description: Mark given 4-digit numbers on number lines: 1043/1069/1084 on a 1000–1100 line; 2025–2460 on a 2000–2500 line; 5512–5695 on a 5500–5725 line; 8679/8990/8923/8763 on an 8500–9000 line.

items.section_title: Breaking up One Thousand — complements and addition facts
items.prompt: A shopkeeper has 650 apples. How many more apples does he need to have exactly 1000?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the complement: 1000 − 650 = 350, or count up from 650 to 1000 in hundreds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark 650 on a hundreds number line and count jumps to 1000; stretch: ask what two different numbers they could add to 650 so the total is still 1000 (e.g. 200 + 150).

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Break Up One-Thousand (a)–(f), p.47
exercise.description: Mark 900, 800, 850, 760, 400 on the Dienes-hundreds number line and find how much more/less each is from 1000; complete eight addition facts of the form ___ + ___ = 1000.

items.section_title: Grouping and Regrouping with Dienes pictures
items.prompt: Rewrite 3 Hundreds, 17 Tens, and 4 Ones as a standard number.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Regroup 17 Tens as 1 Hundred and 7 Tens; then add: 3 + 1 = 4 Hundreds, 7 Tens, 4 Ones = 474.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write 17 Tens as a number (170) and then add 300 + 170 + 4; stretch: ask them to regroup 5 Hundreds, 0 Tens, 23 Ones into standard form.

exercise.description: Identify and write the standard numbers for: 45 Ones, 39 Ones, 35 Tens, 86 Tens, 10T+1O, 15T+23O, 34T+12O, 19T+10O, 2H+13T+7O.

items.section_title: Numbers beyond 1000 — THTO place value, tokens, and sequences
items.prompt: Rewrite 2 Thousands, 15 Hundreds, 3 Tens, and 8 Ones as a standard 4-digit number.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Regroup 15 Hundreds as 1 Thousand and 5 Hundreds; add to get 2+1=3 Thousands, 5 Hundreds, 3 Tens, 8 Ones = 3538.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write 15 Hundreds as a number (1500) and then add 2000 + 1500 + 30 + 8; stretch: ask what the number name for 3538 is and how to write it in expanded form.

exercise.description: Use tokens to identify and write in the Th-H-T-O table: 6T+22O, 4T+12O, 3H+14T+8O, 12H+18T+2O, 1Th+5H+10T+17O.
